title: Pilgrimage: Kushinagar
hookLine: the place of the passing, with a great reclining Buddha

cards: The statue is long, golden, and lying down. Inside a white temple in a small town in northern India, the Buddha rests on his right side, head propped on his hand, eyes almost closed, feet neatly together.
Pilgrims walk slowly around him. Some lay a length of saffron cloth over the body, the way you might tuck a blanket around someone you love. A few people cry; others sit by the wall and chant.
Visitors sometimes take it for the Buddha napping. It isn't. It shows the last hours of his life.
This is Kushinagar, the fourth place the Buddha named as worth a pilgrim's visit.

teach.h: ON HIS RIGHT SIDE, LIKE A LION.
teach.b: The Great Discourse on the Final Passing tells it slowly. First, the posture. Old and ill, the Buddha asks Ananda to set out a couch between twin sal trees, head to the north.
He lies on his right side, one foot on the other, mindful and clear. The text calls it the lion's posture. The trees, it says, burst into bloom out of season and drop their flowers on him.
Ananda goes off alone and weeps. The Buddha sends for him and gently reminds him of what he has always taught: everything dear to us is one day parted from us.

Then he praises Ananda's years of kindness in front of everyone. Third, a latecomer. A wanderer named Subhadda arrives with a question, and Ananda tries to turn him away: do not trouble the teacher, he is weary.
The Buddha overhears, lets him in, and teaches him.
Even at the end, the door stays open. Fourth, the last words. He asks the monks, again and again, whether anyone has a doubt left.

teach.h: WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH DILIGENCE.
teach.b: And then, in Rhys Davids's old translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Buddhists call what followed the parinibbana, the final passing.
Pilgrims come to Kushinagar not only to mourn, but to sit near the place where the teacher, dying, kept teaching.

how: Pilgrims visit Kushinagar in India, walk around the reclining Buddha in the Mahaparinirvana temple, offer robes and flowers, and visit the stupa honored as the place of the cremation.

o: a move to a holy town to spend your last days
a walk to a holy place, made to remember
a march held each year to mourn a teacher

s: the reclining Buddha shows him taking a nap
it shows the last hours of his life, lying on his right side.
at the end, the Buddha asked whether anyone had a doubt left
he asked again and again, and no one spoke.
Ananda stayed perfectly calm at the end
he went off alone and wept, and the Buddha comforted him.

games.q: you're Ananda. your teacher is dying and tired. a stranger arrives at the last hour asking to see him with a question. what do you do?
o: turn him away so the teacher can rest.
games.why: Ananda turned him away, kindly. but the Buddha overheard, called Subhadda in, and taught him. even at the end, the door stayed open.

practice: If your body and space allow, lie on your right side for a minute, one foot resting on the other, head on your hand or a pillow; if not, lean a little to the right in your chair.
Breathe slowly, calm rather than sad, and remember the trees dropping flowers and the teacher who used his last strength to answer one more question. When you're ready, sit up slowly.

wordCard.voice: Pilgrimage. Walking to remember. Its fourth great stop is Kushinagar, where the Buddha passed away between the sal trees. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali parinibbana: the final passing of the Buddha.

carryVoice: Your line: where he passed. Even dying, he kept the door open for one more question. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!
